extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, instructors, and researchers interested in student proof construction and assessment
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing mathematical proofs for their strategic appropriateness — whether the writer chose and deployed techniques, theorems, and modes of argument in a way an experienced mathematician would. Focuses on recognizing and rewarding strategic knowledge in proof construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of powerful proof techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession and use of the standard powerful techniques in the area (e.g., in abstract algebra, showing a subgroup by closure-and-inverse, building a homomorphism with the given kernel, applying the First Isomorphism Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward use of well-established, domain-specific moves rather than reinventing routine arguments; examples: closure-and-inverse for subgroups, constructing homomorphisms to exploit kernel/image theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of which theorems are most important
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that a small number of theorems do most of the work in a typical proof; skilled provers reach for these first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the writer called upon the major, powerful results applicable to the problem rather than relying on many minor lemmas. Prioritize invocation of central theorems when they simplify the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of when particular facts and theorems are likely to be useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Pattern matching from the form of the statement to the relevant tool — knowing when certain facts/theorems are likely to help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess anticipation: did the writer map the problem's structure to familiar patterns and select tools accordingly? Look for signs of recognizing problem types that suggest particular theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of when not to attempt symbol manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing when a proof needs a structural argument rather than direct calculation, and conversely when calculation is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reward choosing the correct mode (structural vs computational). Penalize unnecessary algebraic expansion when a structural fact suffices and penalize hand-wavy structure when explicit computation is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard powerful techniques rather than reinventing
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically well-constructed proof 'uses the standard powerful techniques of its area (rather than reinventing)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the writer reinvented known constructions or leveraged established methods; prefer concision and established methods that are standard practice in the subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach for the right theorems for the statement type
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically well-constructed proof 'reaches for the right theorems for the kind of statement being proved'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate if theorems invoked match the common solution patterns for that statement type; avoid crediting arguments that rely on tangential or weak results instead of central ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the correct mode of argument (structural vs computational)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically well-constructed proof 'recognizes whether the statement calls for symbol manipulation or structural reasoning and proceeds accordingly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the chosen approach aligns with the nature of the claim; penalize mismatches (e.g., using heavy computation on a claim that admits a clean structural proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid brute-force expansion when a structural fact would do
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically well-constructed proof 'avoids brute-force expansion when a structural fact would do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for unnecessary algebraic or index-chasing calculations that could be replaced by invoking an appropriate theorem or structural observation; mark down verbosity and inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid structural hand-waving when explicit calculation would do
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically well-constructed proof 'avoids structural hand-waving when explicit calculation would do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalize vague appeals to structure when the argument demands concrete derivation; require sufficient detail when the structural claim is non-obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does not reprove what standard tools handle
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically poor proof 'reproves something the standard tools handle automatically.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduct for rederiving standard results instead of citing them when appropriate; encourage proper use of known results to streamline proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does not use brute-force where structural argument is cleaner
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically poor proof 'uses a brute-force calculation where a structural argument would be cleaner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and downgrade approaches that rely on lengthy computations in place of succinct structural reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does not mis-identify the type of statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically poor proof 'mis-identifies the type of statement (treating a structural claim as computational, or vice versa)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the student recognized the problem's nature; errors in problem classification that lead to inappropriate methods indicate strategic weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does not invoke minor theorems where major ones apply
rubrics_metrics.description: A strategically poor proof 'invokes minor theorems where major ones apply.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the proof uses weak or tangential results instead of direct application of more powerful theorems; reward judicious selection of strong results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Was the chosen technique appropriate to the problem type?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the technique used matches the problem's classification and typical solution strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a guiding assessment question: appropriateness of method to problem type; consider common archetypal solutions in the subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Were the most powerful relevant theorems invoked?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the writer invoked the strongest applicable theorems rather than relying on weaker or ad-hoc lemmas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit proofs that leverage central theorems efficiently; penalize over-reliance on low-level results when higher-level tools are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Was the mode of argument well-chosen?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess if the writer chose structural reasoning versus computation correctly for the claim at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider clarity, brevity, and match to the claim when judging mode selection; prefer the mode that yields a clearer, more conceptual proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Did the writer recognize the standard form of the problem?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the writer identified the problem as an instance of a familiar pattern that suggests a standard solution route.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of standard forms leads to efficient solution selection; reward identification of analogies and canonical templates within the subfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Would an experienced mathematician have approached it this way?
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-detection criterion: ask whether an experienced mathematician would have approached the problem in the same way; if not, the proof is strategically deficient even if correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert intuition as a benchmark for strategic adequacy. This is a holistic check synthesizing the other criteria — technique choice, theorem selection, and mode of argument.
